AGENTS.md — scrutiny

Source: AGENTS.md

Guidance for AI agents working on the scrutiny R package.

Purpose

scrutiny implements statistical error-detection techniques for published summary statistics — primarily consistency tests GRIM, GRIMMER, and DEBIT. It also provides infrastructure (function factories) for implementing new consistency tests. The package is tidyverse-oriented: tidy data, tibbles throughout (never data.frame()s), and dplyr/purrr idioms.

Style

Avoid overly verbose docs and comments. Don’t write walls of text. Use readable variable names with English words, but still concise ones.

Git

Make one commit each for every medium or major change. In commit messages, don’t use “Co-Authored-By” lines. Start every paragraph after the first line with “*”. Before each commit, run air format on root.

Architecture: the three-tier mapper hierarchy

Every consistency test exists at three levels, each created by a function factory:

*_scalar()          Single-case logic                   (not exported)
*()                 Vectorized, e.g., grim()            map_value_sets()
*_map()             Row-wise test on a data frame       function_map()
*_map_seq()         Dispersed testing around values     function_map_seq()
*_map_total_n()     Testing with unknown group sizes    function_map_total_n()

The factories live in:

Factory File
function_map() R/function-map.R
function_map_seq() R/function-map-seq.R
function_map_total_n() R/function-map-total-n.R
Shared helpers R/function-factory-helpers.R

Each factory uses rlang::new_function() + rlang::expr() to construct the body of the manufactured function at package-load time. !! unquotes a single value into the body; !!! unquote-splices a vector. This is metaprogramming, not string eval — treat the body expressions with care.

The .reported argument to each factory is the character vector of key column names (e.g., c("x", "n") for GRIM, c("x", "sd", "n") for GRIMMER/DEBIT). It drives several automatic behaviours: insert_key_args() adds x = NULL, n = NULL, … to the manufactured function’s formals so users can rename columns; absorb_key_args() applies those renames at call time.

function_map() also has .reported_variadic for tests whose number of key columns is decided by the caller’s data (#42). It names one argument of the *_scalar() function that takes a whole row’s values as a vector; the manufactured function gets an argument by that name which selects columns with tidyselect::eval_select() at call time. The selected columns are returned as themselves, so the output shape is unchanged. Such a mapper is basic-tier only: function_map_seq() and function_map_total_n() derive their own arguments from .reported, so check_fn_wrappable() refuses it, as it refuses result columns named like those the tier adds. add_up_to_map() is the one mapper built with it.

All three basic mappers — grim_map(), grimmer_map(), debit_map() — are one-liners calling function_map(), as the seq and total-n mappers have always been. There is no handwritten mapper left in the package. Everything the three need is expressed declaratively through these function_map() arguments:

Argument Purpose
.args_by_row args with one value per row (digits_x, digits_sd); become output columns
.args_fixed values always passed to the *_scalar() function, with no argument exposed for them (grimmer_map()’s show_reason = TRUE); passing one is a “disabled argument” error
.cols_helper args that may also be data columns (items_averaged, data_type); returned as a column right after the key columns if given, as an argument or a column, and not returned at all if left at the default. A helper with no default must be given one way or the other
.col_names names for the values a *_scalar() function returns under show_rec / show_reason
.cols_derived columns computed from the same input but not returned by the *_scalar() function (exp_incon ← grim_exp_incon()); each function is vectorized and called once per mapper call

Every other argument of the *_scalar() function automatically becomes a real formal of the manufactured function with the same default — not a dots argument. This is load-bearing: see the digits_* section below. The seq and total-n factories follow suit: formals_settings() (R/function-factory-helpers.R) copies .fn’s settings — its formals after the dots, such as rounding — with .fn’s defaults. Before #95 these went through the dots, hidden from formals() and the help page. No mapper’s dots take anything now; they only force the arguments after them to be named in full.

A setting whose default is a set of strings, such as sd_meaning = c("sd_sample", "sd_pop", "sd_sample_or_pop", "se"), is an “enum” (is_enum_default()). function_map() reassigns one left at its default to the first value before anything else reads it, so the length check, the *_scalar() function, and the "scrutiny" attribute all see a single string. One given as the whole set, as a wrapper forwarding its own default does, is resolved the same way by resolve_enums(), in function_map(), map_value_sets(), and function_map_total_n(), which reads sd_meaning for n_min before fn() runs. The *_scalar() functions check enums against constants in R/aaa.R (SD_MEANINGS, DEBIT_FORMULAS) rather than their own formals, which is cheaper per row; a test in test-utils.R requires every default to equal its constant.

sd_meaning is one argument on purpose: each value is one premise about what a value reported as an SD really is (sd_* values: an SD of that kind; "se": a misreported SE). It replaced sd_type before 1.0.0 rather than gaining a second, combinable argument, because few combinations of statistic and denominator occur in practice. sd_denominator(n, sd_meaning) maps each premise to the number the sum of squared deviations is divided by to give the reported value squared; every place that turns the reported value into a sum of squares or a binary spread goes through it, so a new premise of the same form is one row there, plus one in sd_denominator_ratio(), which the sd_binary_*() functions use to stay finite for huge n; a test requires the two to agree. "var" would not be: its bounds are not squared. Functions that return values under one premise, such as grimmer_values() and sd_binary_*(), reject "sd_sample_or_pop" via check_sd_meaning_single().

Arguments deliberately not carried over in the migration, because they were sugar over one dplyr verb and blocked the unification: extra (→ dplyr::select() on the output), testables_only (→ dplyr::filter(exp_incon > 0)), and merge_items = FALSE, which produced a packed n column that nothing downstream can read. Don’t reintroduce them. Nor grimmer_map(show_reason), which only dropped a column; it is .args_fixed now. grim_map() and debit_map() keep show_rec, whose default is FALSE: the reconstructed numbers are intermediate results that few readers cite. debit_plot() needs them and recomputes them under the recorded settings if they are missing.

grim_map() and grimmer_map() no longer multiply items into n. The n column is the sample size as given, and grim_plot_grid() places tiles at n * items_averaged.

items_averaged replaced items before 1.0.0 (#94) and, like digits_x, has no default: the old default of 1 let multi-item scales pass as single items, and “items” was mistaken for the number of scale points. A missing one reaches the *_scalar() function as missing, which calls error_items_missing() (R/utils.R) after the digits_* checks. In mappers, manage_helper_col() is then called without default, and an items_averaged column of data satisfies the requirement. Only grim_granularity() keeps a default; it is no test.

data_type (DATA_TYPES in R/aaa.R: "integer", "continuous") is a second helper of GRIM and GRIMMER, and DEBIT’s only one, with no default, for the same reason: the tests only apply to whole numbers (for DEBIT, 0 and 1). A missing one calls error_data_type_missing(). The *_scalar() functions pass anything but "integer" to test_data_type() (R/utils.R), which returns verdict_continuous()’s result for continuous data and applies the NA rule to a missing value. The *_explain() functions do the same through explain_data_type(), and grim_total() returns 0 for continuous data, so exp_incon follows; it and grim_exp_incon() require data_type too. grim_plot_grid() and debit_plot() leave continuous rows out via drop_continuous(). The functions that list or draw the values whole numbers can have (*_values(), *_closest(), *_plot_line()) require data_type too, so that every call states the assumption, but "continuous" is an error there (check_data_type_whole()); grim_grid() follows grim(). GRIM’s x_meaning ("mean" or "percentage", X_MEANINGS) replaced the logical percent before 1.0.0; it is an enum like sd_meaning. The exports without dots keep percent = deprecated() to call stop_percent(), and check_factory_dots() calls it for the mappers.

The digits_* argument pattern

Since v0.6, x and sd are stored as numeric (not character strings). The number of decimal places therefore cannot be inferred from the value itself and must be supplied explicitly.

  • grim_map() requires digits_x (no default).
  • grimmer_map() requires both digits_x and digits_sd.
  • debit_map() requires both digits_x and digits_sd.

A mapper also takes them from digits_* columns of data if the arguments are left out: a column states them as explicitly as an argument. function_map() reads such columns like any .args_by_row argument; the seq factory reads them back from its initial fn() call’s output, one per row, and disperses each case on its own decimal level; the total-n factory carries them along with the other columns of data, so a row’s value applies to both groups.

If digits_x is missing, the scalar function calls error_digits_missing(x) (R/utils.R) which gives a context-aware error message with an example fix. Do not replace this with a generic R missing-argument error.

check_newly_numeric(x, digits_x) (R/utils.R) validates that digits_x is consistent with x.

How digits_* flows through the factory stack

function_map_seq() computes digits_args_names as the intersection of paste0("digits_", .reported[.reported != "n"]) with names(formals(.fn)). This means digits_x is auto-added to grim_map_seq(), grimmer_map_seq(), and debit_map_seq() (all three now require the corresponding digits_* args).

Inside the manufactured function body the digits args are collected into digits_vals via Filter(Negate(is.null), mget(...)) and forwarded through both the initial do.call(fn, c(list(data), digits_vals, list(...))) call and the per-variable map_seq_proto calls via fn_args <- c(digits_vals, list(...)).

Key files by subsystem

Core tests

File Content
R/grim.R grim_scalar() — single-case GRIM logic using roundwork::sum_range()
R/grimmer.R grimmer_scalar() — Analytic-GRIMMER, whose test 1 also requires at least sum_squares_min(), the smallest sum of squares that whole numbers with the candidate sum can have, and for n < 5 one that sum_squares_attainable() admits. For n >= 5, minimum and parity suffice, so the verdict is exact. Scale bounds (#60) were cut before 1.0.0 in favor of strait (#88)
R/debit.R debit_scalar() / debit(), plus the DEBIT input-range checks
R/grimmer-sum-squares.R sd_square_term(), sum_squares_range_shifted(), sum_squares_min(), sum_squares_attainable() (which sums of squares fewer than five whole numbers can have; see special-scripts/grimmer-attainable-sums-of-squares.qmd), and sum_squares_attainable_all(), all of them in a range — GRIMMER’s exact sum-of-squares arithmetic. The rules for three and four numbers live in sum_squares_attainable_all() only, vectorized over windows; for three, loeschian_between() generates the numbers x^2 + xy + y^2 rather than testing each. The rounding bounds behind all three tests come from roundwork::bound_numerators() and roundwork::sum_range() (gotcha 6)
R/grim-values.R grim_values(), grim_closest() — the achievable means behind a reported one; both thin wrappers over roundwork::sum_range(). grim_values() returns one tibble (case, x, sum), like grimmer_values(), stacked by bind_cases() from the per-set tibbles: an inconsistent value set has no rows, an undecidable one a row of NA. More than VALUES_MAX rows for one value set is an error from check_values_size() (R/utils.R), raised before they are allocated
R/debit-values.R debit_values() — every number of ones whose mean and SD would be reported as the given ones; the k range from roundwork::sum_range(), filtered by binary_spread_range(), as in debit_scalar(). formula = "mean_n" and sd_meaning = "sd_sample_or_pop" are errors there: no finite list, and two premises. debit_closest() picks the SD closest to sd from these, from the k whose mean rounds to x, or from grim_closest()’s k, in that order
R/grimmer-values.R grimmer_values() — every (mean, SD) pair behind a reported one, with the whole-number sum and sum of squares; takes the verdict from grimmer_scalar(), then enumerates through grimmer_candidate() and sum_squares_attainable(). "sd_sample_or_pop" is an error there: one premise per call. For n < 5 the pairs can’t be counted without finding them, so they are counted as found, against VALUES_MAX. grimmer_closest() finds the pair whose SD is closest to sd without listing any: per remainder modulo n, the sum of squares nearest the target (closest_square_parity(), vectorized, for n >= 5; closest_square_few() below)
R/grim-explain.R, R/grimmer-explain.R, R/debit-explain.R *_explain() — one case in plain words. Built from the numbers that decide the test: grim_scalar(show_rec = TRUE), grimmer_candidate(), binary_spread_range(); GRIMMER and DEBIT abort on disagreement with the verdict
R/explain-map.R explain_map(), a generic like audit(), with methods for the three basic mappers’ classes, which also covers the seq and total-n tiers. Not explain(): that name is taken by dplyr, DALEX, and lime. Adds an explanation column of format()ed explanations. Re-tests each row with the settings from scrutiny_args() and errors if the verdict differs from the row’s consistency
R/explain-print.R explain_print() — cat()s the explanation column, with rows picked as in dplyr::slice(), always calling explain_map() on these rows, so that a user’s own explanation column is refused rather than printed. Other classes reach explain_map.default(), which errors, so packages can add methods; the check is not is_map_df(), which also admits add_up_to_map() etc. explain_print() itself only checks for a tibble
R/map-value-sets.R map_value_sets(), recycle_length_common() — the shared body of grim(), grimmer(), debit(), grim_values(), grim_closest(), percentage_of(), and add_up_to(): applies a *_scalar() function once per value set, taking the caller’s arguments

Decimal handling

decimal_places() counts from the string representation. Numeric values lose trailing zeros, so always pass strings when exact decimal counts matter (e.g., "3.70" gives 2; 3.70 gives 1).

File Content

The generic is audit(data, ..., .by = NULL), so every method takes (data, ...). .by never reaches a method: audit_by() splits with [, which keeps class and attribute, and calls audit() per group. group_by() keeps the attribute but drops the class, and ungroup() drops both; making the class survive would take methods for several dplyr verbs per class. hint_grouped() names the cause in audit.default() and explain_map.default() instead

S3 class system

Mapper output carries multiple classes stacked as a character vector:

c("scrutiny_grim_map", "tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")

Classes are for dispatch only. Settings of the call that functions downstream need live in one list attribute, "scrutiny". Its settings element is a tibble built by new_settings() (R/function-factory-helpers.R): setting, value (a list-column of the values themselves), default, and added_by. function_map() writes the basic mapper’s rows — every argument that applied to the whole call, defaults resolved — and the seq and total-n factories append their own, such as dispersion. default compares each value to the defaults that eval_defaults() evaluated when the factory made the mapper; added_by is name_mapper()’s guess from .name_test ("grim_map"), since a manufactured function doesn’t know the name it was assigned to.

Package code reads typed values with the internal scrutiny_args(), which returns the basic mapper’s rows as a named list — rounding selects grim_plot_grid()’s raster, x_meaning makes it apply the test’s conversion (divide x by 100, raise the decimal count by 2). The exported scrutiny_meta() is for people: it returns the tibble with value written as code in single quotes, because pillar quotes and escapes a whole character column as soon as one value has a double quote in it. Don’t read it in package code. .args_fixed values are not recorded: they are settings of the mapper, not of the call. Attributes and classes survive exactly the same dplyr verbs, so the move changed nothing there; it replaced regex parsing of class strings and made accidental dispatch on a flag impossible. Storing all the arguments rather than a chosen few is what made .name_class_flags unnecessary. Don’t add flag classes again.

  • scrutiny_{test}_map — drives audit() dispatch, and the pillar::tbl_sum() methods in R/scrutiny-meta.R, which add a header line naming the settings whose default is FALSE. pillar pads header names to the widest, so the lines are returned unnamed with the names pasted in. A new basic mapper needs such a method to get the line
  • scrutiny_map_seq / scrutiny_map_total_n — the generic tier classes; these are what audit_seq() and audit_total_n() dispatch on
  • scrutiny_{test}_map_seq / scrutiny_{test}_map_total_n — the test-specific tier classes. They exist so that users can write their own S3 methods for one particular mapper’s output. The total-n half was documented in ?audit-special but never set until the 1.0.0 audit fixes; function_map_total_n() now adds it the way function_map_seq() always has.

*_map_seq() output takes the "scrutiny" attribute of its initial fn() call and adds its own settings rows and elements to it (see gotcha 16), setting it explicitly after assembly rather than relying on it to survive purrr::list_rbind(). Total-n output does the same with the attribute of its "forth" half, plus a reported element: the statistics reported for both groups, which reverse_map_total_n() reads because a custom basic mapper may put n anywhere among its key columns.

grim_plot_grid() and mixed decimal places

grim_map(), grimmer_map(), debit_map(), and every mapper built on top of them (*_map_seq(), *_map_total_n()) attach the digits_x (and, where applicable, digits_sd) they were given as an output column. grim_plot_grid() reads decimal places from that column instead of guessing via decimal_places(data$x), which is unreliable for numeric x: trailing zeros are lost, so 5.00 reads back as 0 decimal places, not 2 (see gotcha 6 below). Guessing from x is only a fallback for data with no digits_x column, e.g. a hand-built tibble.

grim_plot_grid() errors by default if the decimal counts still differ across rows after that (i.e. the data itself mixes decimal places), because the background raster is only meaningful for one specific decimal count, and a single call should have a stable return type (one ggplot, not sometimes a ggplot and sometimes a list). Set split_by_digits = TRUE to opt into the alternative: grim_plot_grid() then splits the data by distinct non-zero digits_x values, produces one plot per group, and returns a named list (list(digits_1 = ..., digits_2 = ...)) invisibly. Each plot is also printed as a side-effect. A cli::cli_alert_success() message reports the count and decimal values when more than one plot is made.

function_map_seq() internals — things to know

function_map_seq_proto() (the inner helper factory) manufactures a per-variable test function. Its inner function has ... that are forwarded to fn(...). These ... are not the outer function’s dots — they come from the call site of the proto function.

The outer fn_out body captures the arguments given (e.g., digits_x, rounding) into fn_args <- c(digits_vals, setting_vals, list(...)) and forwards them via do.call(map_seq_proto, c(list(data = data, var = variable), fn_args)). If you need to add new args that must reach fn(), include them in fn_args or make them explicit args like the digits_* treatment above.

digits_* columns are added to the output for every non-n reported variable (e.g., digits_x for GRIM, digits_x + digits_sd for GRIMMER/DEBIT) and relocated to appear immediately before consistency.

Limits that depend on a setting are functions of the resolved settings, as a named list. function_map_seq() takes them as .var_bounds (n = function(args) c(sd_min_n(args$sd_meaning), NA) in the GRIMMER and DEBIT seq mappers), function_map_total_n() as .n_min; there the manufactured function’s n_min defaults to NULL, which the body resolves, and the resolved value is what the recorded setting counts as the default. A constant works in both places as before.

Coding conventions

  • Tibbles: always use tibble::tibble(), or, in performance-sensitive cases where nrow is known, tibble::new_tibble(); never data.frame().
  • Error messages: cli::cli_abort() with named vector elements ("!", "x", "i"). Never stop(). For errors about user input, use abort_in_export(), which names the exported function the user called, wherever on the stack the check runs; name_last_export() gives that name for the message text. Never count frames. Every error that is not a bug in scrutiny goes through it; an internal error, one that only a bug can cause, is cli::cli_abort(..., .internal = TRUE). These come from R/import-standalone-last-export.R, imported from unsum with usethis::use_standalone(): change them upstream, never by hand.
  • Warnings/info: cli::cli_warn() / cli::cli_inform().
  • Scalar helpers: functions that operate on a single case are named *_scalar() and not exported. They have a thin vectorized wrapper, e.g., grim().
  • File naming: matches the exported function with - not _ as separator (e.g., grim-map-seq.R exports grim_map_seq()).
  • Constants: package-level constants live in R/aaa.R and are named in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, so that a name elsewhere is recognizable as one on sight. They are evaluated at install time, which for the tolerance is deliberate: a verdict must not depend on the machine. R/aaa.R is first in Collate because roxygen2 sorts unconstrained files alphabetically.
  • @include roxygen tag: used to guarantee correct NAMESPACE order; do not remove existing @include directives unless you intend to change collate order.
  • check_factory_dots(): called near the top of every manufactured function body. It checks that ... args are valid formals of fn. Args that are explicit named params (like digits_x) are not in ... and therefore not checked here — that is expected.
  • No function written inside dplyr::across() that reads a variable. dplyr inlines it, and the variable is then looked up among the columns of data first: a column named sep replaced the argument of split_by_parens(). Define the function before the mutate() call.
  • integer64 is rejected, not converted. It is a double by type, so is.numeric() is TRUE, but only bit64 can read its values. check_not_integer64() (R/utils.R) runs once per call: by name in function_map() for the tested columns and in map_value_sets(), and in round_whole() for every other export that takes a whole number.
  • Numbers become strings through number_to_string() (R/decimal-places.R), never a bare as.character() whose result is parsed: that writes the decimal mark of options(OutDec = ).
  • Never rlang::enexprs(...) where a value is needed. Inside a manufactured function body, capturing the dots as expressions yields the caller’s expression — a symbol if the caller passed a variable — unless the promises happen to have been forced already. Use list(...) for values. The seq factory’s rounding-class fixup got this wrong once and only worked by accident.

Testing

Tests live in tests/testthat/. The framework is testthat >= 3.0.0.

  • helper.R — general helpers: unclass_scr(), censor(), integer_places(), sweep_seed() (a new seed per run outside of CRAN; SCRUTINY_SEED replays one)
  • The full DEBIT oracle in test-debit.R runs only with SCRUTINY_FULL_ORACLE=true, as in the weekly .github/workflows/full-oracle.yaml
  • test-mapper-oracle.R re-tests every row of every mapper tier with the vectorized test; a new setting or mapper belongs there too. See special-scripts/oracle-tests-assessment.md for all the sweeps
  • helper-expectations.R — custom expectations: expect_na()
  • Snapshot tests use testthat::expect_snapshot(); regenerate with testthat::snapshot_review() when output changes intentionally.

Test style

Follow commit c3abc01 (test-utils.R) as the model:

  • A pipe chain starts with the object, never with a call on it: write x |> f1() |> f2(), not f1(x) |> f2(). Only a compound first argument (list(a, b), c(...), tibble::tibble(...)) starts the chain as a call.
  • Expectations go at the end of the chain: x |> f(y = 1) |> expect_error("msg"), not expect_error(f(x, y = 1), "msg").
  • Several |> on one line are fine, and preferred: don’t break a line after a pipe. A chain that is broken after one pipe is broken after every pipe — never half and half.
  • In consecutive parallel lines, align the pipes with spaces to show the parallels. air.toml skips test_that() blocks, so the formatter leaves them alone there; at the top level, end each aligned (or over-long parallel) line with # fmt: skip.
  • Leave expect_snapshot() code alone; the snapshot files record it.

When modifying a factory (function-map-seq.R etc.), run tests for all three mappers that use it (GRIM, GRIMMER, DEBIT), not just the one under immediate focus.

Gotchas and non-obvious behaviours

  1. digits_x has no default in grim_map() / grimmer_map(). Calling them without it, and without a digits_x column in data, hits error_digits_missing(), not a generic R error. This is intentional — the error message guides users.

  2. seq_disperse_df_internal() is a lightweight version of seq_disperse_df() used inside function_map_seq_proto(). Both wrap seq_disperse(), so a fix there reaches the mappers too. out_min and out_max apply to from itself as well: a reported value outside of them is dropped even under include_reported = TRUE, so seq_disperse(0) has no "0" under the default out_min = "auto".

  3. grim_map_seq() et al. are one-liners that call function_map_seq(). There is no hand-written function body. All logic lives in the factory. When debugging manufactured functions, check the factory body in R/function-map-seq.R, not the one-liner in R/grim-map-seq.R.

  4. *_map_seq() output records the settings of the initial fn() call, such as rounding with its default resolved, by copying that call’s "scrutiny" attribute onto the assembled output. The re-tests get the same arguments, so the record holds for every row.

  5. insert_key_args() inserts after data and the digits_* args — insert_after = 1L + length(<by-row args>) in all three factories. The digits_* args have no defaults and must be given in every call, so they sit next to data, in the same position in every mapper. The dots come right after the key arguments, so every argument after them must be named in full: items = 2 partially matched items_averaged, and n in a total-n mapper both n_min and n_max. The total-n mappers have an n key argument for the column of totals. Final signature order: data, digits_x, x, n, ..., items_averaged, data_type, … for grim_map(), data, digits_x, x, n, ..., items_averaged, data_type, x_meaning, …, var, dispersion, … for grim_map_seq(), and data, digits_x, x1, x2, n, ..., items_averaged, data_type, x_meaning, …, dispersion, … for grim_map_total_n(): the basic mapper’s settings come right after the helpers in all three tiers. function_map() reorders formals_promoted to put the .args_by_row args first; do that after args_required is derived, since that line pairs formals_promoted with args_promoted by position.

    Each factory works out its own digits_args_names as the intersection of paste0("digits_", <its reported vars>) with names(formals(.fn)), so a test that takes no decimal places at all gets no such arguments. The total-n factory took them through the dots until the 1.0.0 audit fixes: that worked, and the missing-argument error was still the bespoke one, but the argument was invisible to formals(), to tab-completion, and to the rendered help page.

    Helper arguments got the same treatment for the same reason. The seq and total-n factories read .fn’s "scrutiny_args_helper" attribute and copy those formals with .fn’s defaults, so items_averaged has none there either. The body collects the ones given into helper_vals as its very first step, before any local could shadow one, and leaves out missing ones so that they reach fn() as missing. The seq factory passes them to the initial fn() call only, not to fn_args: the re-tests read them from the column that call returned.

    The settings (formals_settings()) are collected into setting_vals the same way, right after helper_vals, but go to both the initial call and fn_args. One left out is not forwarded, so fn() applies its own default, which is the same.

  6. Rounding lives in roundwork. reround(), unround(), the round_*() functions, bound_numerators(), sum_range(), and resolve_ties_rounding() are roundwork’s, called as roundwork::*(). Fix rounding there, not here: until 1.0.0, scrutiny had its own copy, and the two drifted apart by some 90 commits. bound_numerators(), sum_range(), and resolve_ties_rounding() are low-level primitives that check little of their input, so scrutiny checks it before calling them.

    roundwork does check rounding, threshold, and symmetric, but its errors name the roundwork function that scrutiny called, such as sum_range(). Every scrutiny export that takes them therefore calls check_rounding_args() (R/utils.R) once, before any per-row work: via map_value_sets(), the function_map() body, the *_explain() functions, and grim_plot_grid(). It asks roundwork for the bounds of a stand-in value and re-raises any error through rethrow_in_export() as one from the user’s export. A new export with a rounding argument needs this too, unless it goes through one of those.

  7. The "ties_*" rounding methods are shorthand. Each names a complete tie-breaking procedure, so it stands in for a rounding plus a symmetric, and giving symmetric = TRUE with one is an error. Anything in scrutiny that branches on rounding itself has to resolve them with roundwork::resolve_ties_rounding() — grim_plot_grid() does, to pick the background raster. The oracle grid in test-grim-oracle.R skips symmetric for these methods, which costs no coverage: the name alone decides them.

  8. No rounding method has undefined bounds. roundwork::bound_numerators() returns NULL only for a missing or infinite x. "anti_trunc" at zero used to be another case, and much of the package’s NA-propagation machinery was written with it as the example; since anti_trunc() became ceiling(abs(x)) (matching Excel’s ROUNDUP()), zero has the single-point range 0 <= x <= 0. Use a missing value or a non-positive n when you need an undecidable case.

  9. decimal_places() counts from string representation. Numeric 3.70 returns 1, not 2. This means digits_x from decimal_places(x) on a numeric column can be wrong if trailing zeros have been lost. In *_map() and *_map_seq() output the digits_x column is not computed via decimal_places() on the values — it is set directly from the digits_x argument provided by the caller (via recycle_digits() in the basic mappers) and replicated for every output row. This is reliable even when trailing zeros have been lost from the numeric x column.

    Non-finite values return NA, not 0: NaN is a missing value everywhere in the package, and an infinity has no decimal places to count. decimal_places() decides this from the input — is.finite() for a numeric vector, a case-insensitive match against the inf, infinity, and nan tokens for a character one, plus the exact string "NA", which restore_zeros() reads as missing too — because as.numeric() would also swallow strings like "5.30%", whose two decimal places are the documented answer. decimal_places_scalar() has to agree with it; a generated corpus in test-decimal-places.R checks that they do.

    Two rules say which strings are missing, by what a function reads (R/aaa.R, at NON_FINITE_TOKENS): functions that read numbers from strings follow as.numeric(), so "nan" and "inf" in any letter case are non-finite; functions that read any text, such as duplicate_count(), take only "NaN" as R writes it, via is_value_missing(), because "Nan" is a name. Don’t unify them.

    An all-NA vector of any type is NA of the argument’s type: na_as_integer() (R/utils.R), called from round_whole() and as_integer_if_lossless(), turns a logical or character NA column of n, items_averaged, or digits_x into NA_integer_, and na_as_character() does the same for data_type (ARGS_STRING). A NULL or an empty vector is left alone: NULL means “none” to disperse_total(n_max). A digits_* column of strings is refused up front by check_digits_numeric(), since every row would fail and the per-row error would blame none.

  10. absorb_key_args() modifies data before any other processing. If you add pre-processing that reads column names, it must happen after this call. It reads the key arguments’ values in the calling mapper’s frame (capture_key_args(), via rlang::enquo()), never the unevaluated call: through lapply() the call is FUN(X[[i]], ...), and from a wrapper it names a variable. A bare name is a column name if data has that column, else the string a variable of that name holds. A key argument pointing elsewhere while data already has a column of the argument’s own name is an error, not silently ignored.

  11. write_code_col_key_result() is called at the very end of manufactured function bodies. It may rename the consistency column and coerces list-columns to logical. Any column additions/relocations must happen before this call. Only function_map() passes rename = TRUE (the default): it is the tier that creates the column. The seq and total-n factories build on a basic mapper’s output, where the column already carries its final name, and pass rename = FALSE so that only the unlist() half of the generated code applies.

    .name_key_result is threaded through all three factories. Everything that reads the key result column off .fn’s output does so by that name — the seq factory’s filter of consistent cases and its digits_* relocation, function_map_total_n_proto()’s mutate_both_consistent(), audit_seq(), and reverse_map_seq(). The last two learn the name from the name_key_result element of the "scrutiny" attribute that function_map_seq() puts on its output, falling back to "consistency" when the attribute is gone. A mapper and its sequence or total-n mapper must be created with the same .name_key_result; check_key_result_col() says so if they were not.

  12. Every mapper applies its test to the first row on its own, before mapping over all of them. Arguments of a *_scalar() function without a default (i.e., digits_x and digits_sd) must reach it as missing, so that error_digits_missing() fires rather than a generic R error; function_map() therefore skips them when collecting the arguments to pass down. The pre-application is what keeps the resulting error out of purrr::pmap()’s indexed-error context, and it runs unconditionally: anything wrong with the arguments themselves fails on the first row just as it would on any other. The rounding arguments are checked even before that (gotcha 6). It used to run only for missing required arguments.

    Do not muffle warnings or messages in that call. It looks right, since the row is about to be tested again, but a once-per-session warning is then lost for good: lifecycle::deprecate_warn() records that it has warned before the muffle discards the warning, so the deprecated grim_map(tolerance) (removed before 1.0.0) went through in complete silence. Nothing on the scalar test path warns per row today.

    An error in any later row still comes from inside purrr::pmap(), which wraps it in an “In index: 14” context naming its own anonymous function. rethrow_row_error() (R/mapper-function-helpers.R) re-signals the test’s own error instead, with an “In row 14 of data” bullet and a scrutiny_row field. The total-n proto function reads that field and rewrites the bullet to the row of the user’s data, since a row of its rebuilt data is a hypothetical scenario.

    An error in the first row goes through signal_in_row() too, but only if some other row passes (passes_any_row(), which tries rows 2 to 50 and the last): an error about the arguments, such as a missing digits_x, fails on every row and must not blame row 1.

  13. special-scripts/ contains development aids and GRIMMER debugging material. It is not part of the built package. special-scripts/dormant/ holds the rivets and metadata files that used to sit in R/ as ~1,500 lines of fully commented-out code, ~9% of the package’s source, walked through by every reader, grep, and coverage tool. Put unfinished work there, not in R/.

  14. grim_map(show_rec = TRUE) returns the same columns for every rounding method: rec_sum, sum_lower, sum_upper, rec_x_upper, rec_x_lower. sum_lower/sum_upper come straight from the sum_range() call that decided consistency, so display and verdict cannot come apart. Up to 1.0.0 the columns were the two granules re-rounded — a second derivation of the verdict, which under rounding = "anti_trunc" could contradict it. Don’t reintroduce a display that is computed separately from the verdict.

  15. Zero-row input. write_result_cols() cannot read the output’s shape off a result that doesn’t exist, so a mapper called on a 0-row data tests a row of missing values instead and returns the columns of that result with no rows. If .fn fails on missing values, only the key result column is returned. Total-n output with no pair of group sizes gets its columns the same way. A *_map_seq() call with no inconsistent case returns 0 rows too, but with the usual columns, classes, and attribute, so audit_seq() and reverse_map_seq() accept it. Undecidable cases are never dispersed, not even under include_consistent = TRUE; the warning counts them.

  16. Attributes tie the mapper tiers together. function_map() records its helper-column argument names (e.g., items_averaged) as the "scrutiny_args_helper" attribute of the mapper it manufactures. A helper that was given is a column of the mapper’s output, so function_map_seq() keeps the helper args out of the arguments forwarded to the re-tests, which read them from the column, and function_map_total_n() carries such columns into the data it rebuilds for fn(). Until 1.0.0, grim_map() multiplied items into n and both factories had to undo that; GRIMMER uses n - 1 and items^2, so testing the product gave wrong verdicts. The seq mapper in turn records the verdict of every input row from its initial fn() call as the results_reported element of the "scrutiny" attribute of its output. audit_seq() reports these for the cases present, indexed by case, instead of re-testing reconstructed data: until the 1.0.0 design review it recovered the mapper’s name from a class string, looked the function up in the caller’s environment, and replayed the call’s arguments from a fn_args element, so a dropped argument could flip the verdict and the mapper had to be findable from wherever audit_seq() ran. Verbs like summarise() and pivot_longer() drop the attribute ([, filter(), and bind_rows() keep it, the last only for pieces of one output: R/bind-rows.R registers vctrs methods that reject output of different calls, whose settings or verdicts differ, or rows of a plain data frame; base rbind() is not covered. Column binding passes: vec_cbind() asks the same methods with zero-column inputs); audit_seq() then errors, like explain_map(). The same attribute holds name_key_result (see gotcha 11). No order of dispersion steps needs recording: each row’s diff_var says how far it was moved. var, the dispersed variables, from which audit_seq() shapes its output when there are no rows, is a row of settings. Seq and total-n output also record values_reported, the key columns of their input: their case numbers restart at 1 per call, so without it two calls with the same settings would pass the bind_rows() guard. They also record the rows of each group, rows_dispersed per case and var and rows_tested per case and dir (count_rows_by(), R/audit.R): a group with fewer rows lost some to filter() or the like, so audit_seq() and audit_total_n() say NA for it. add_up_to_map() records cols_variadic, the columns its summands selected.

  17. A test that cannot be decided says NA, and all three agree on what those cases are. is_decidable_n_items() (R/utils.R) is the single condition — stated twice, in && form for the single values the *_scalar() functions pass it once per row and in & form for the columns grim_exp_incon() passes it once per call. The two have to be kept identical; a test in test-utils.R runs both over the same grid and requires them to agree. Do not collapse them into one: && neither allocates nor evaluates what it does not need, which is most of the per-row cost, and looping the scalar form over a column would cost far more than it saves. The condition itself: n and items_averaged must be positive whole numbers, and n must be at least 2 for GRIMMER and DEBIT, which reconstruct a sample SD and so divide by n - 1. GRIM’s min_n is 1 — the mean of a single value is that value.

    A missing x or sd (or digits_x/digits_sd) is NA only if it could decide the case either way. GRIMMER with sd missing is FALSE if x fails GRIM; with x missing, it checks the sums 0:(n - 1), which stand for all sums by their remainder modulo n, and is FALSE if none admits the SD. DEBIT with sd missing is FALSE if no number of ones rounds to x ("exact" only); with x missing, if no number of ones (or, under "mean_n", no mean) has the SD. combine_sd_sample_or_pop() keeps "sd_sample_or_pop" at NA when the sample SD is open and the population SD fails. The *_explain() functions have paragraphs for these cases. A value whose digits_* is missing has at least the decimal places it shows (digits_least(), R/utils.R), and more only narrow its rounding range: if the value set is FALSE with these, it is FALSE. If it is TRUE with so many that only the value shown passes (digits_exact_mean(), digits_exact_sd()), it is TRUE; not under DEBIT’s "mean_n". Else the value counts as missing. A negative SD is FALSE even with n missing. A missing n or items_averaged gives TRUE if a value set passes with 1 in its place (GRIM: copies of the values keep the mean; GRIMMER and DEBIT: data that are all the same, with an SD of 0), and with n missing, GRIMMER and DEBIT give FALSE for an SD below sd_below_floor()’s floor or, for DEBIT, above the largest a binary sample can have (debit_n_missing()). GRIM with x missing is TRUE if every mean passes (grim_all_means_pass()). grim_exp_incon() stays NA for a missing n: its number depends on it. The rule is frozen there: vignette("technical-notes"), section Missing values, lists the cases that stay NA although every value would give the same result, and ?grim, ?grimmer, and ?debit point to it. A change to these cases needs that list changed too.

    The tolerance accepts a value like 100 * 0.29 (28.999999999999996) as whole, so it is also tested as 29: round_whole() (R/utils.R) rounds the ARGS_WHOLE arguments (R/aaa.R) at the export boundaries, before any arithmetic or comparison with min_n – function_map()’s cols_tested, map_value_sets(), the *_explain() and *_plot_line() functions, grim_total() and grim_exp_incon(), the sd_binary_*() functions, disperse() and disperse_total(), and the total-n body’s data$n. A new export that reads these arguments itself, rather than through one of those, needs the same call. The *_scalar() functions never see the noise. Fractional values are left alone and rejected as before.

    That 2 is sd_min_n(sd_meaning) since #95: sd_meaning = "sd_pop" divides by n (sd_denominator(), R/utils.R), so n = 1 is testable there. "sd_sample_or_pop" re-runs the *_scalar() function under both conventions: TRUE if the sample SD passes, otherwise the population SD’s verdict. That is | everywhere except at n = 1, where no sample SD exists, so it cannot leave the verdict NA. The re-run comes after the missing(digits_*) checks on purpose: a missing argument passed on from a closure is no longer missing() in the callee, so error_digits_missing() would not fire. sd_meaning and formula are validated with arg_match_in_export(sd_meaning, SD_MEANINGS) etc., whose fast path is ~8 times cheaper per row than a bare rlang::arg_match().

    Before the 1.0.0 audit fixes each test made its own arrangements and none of them covered fractional input: grim(x = 5.19, n = 20.5) was FALSE, grimmer(items = 1.5) was TRUE, grimmer(n = 1) was FALSE through a NaN that na.rm = TRUE swallowed, and debit(n = 1) was FALSE through an Inf that compared as “above the upper bound”. grim_exp_incon() uses the same condition, so the exp_incon column cannot report a number next to an NA verdict.

  18. grim_plot_grid() returns its plot; it does not print it. The one exception is the split_by_digits = TRUE branch, which returns a list that auto-printing cannot draw, so it prints each plot itself and returns the list invisibly. The function used to end on print() unconditionally, which drew a canvas nobody asked for whenever the result was assigned, added to, or composed.

    It also reports what it leaves out rather than letting ggplot2 drop rows: value sets whose consistency is NA have no color to be drawn in, and digits_x = 0 rows have a fractional portion of zero and no raster. Both are warnings naming the count; if nothing is left, that is an error.

  19. data <- as_tibble_input(data) is the first statement in every manufactured mapper body — in all three factories, ahead of absorb_key_args() and of anything else that reads column names. It admits any data frame and returns a tibble, keeping character row names as a rowname column (integer ones, as left by data[rows, ], are dropped, and a rowname column next to row names is an error); anything else is an error. Keep it first. A non-data-frame has no column names to speak of, so a key-column check running ahead of it reports missing columns and blames the user’s data for the wrong object — worst of all for an undefined data, which R resolves to utils::data(). Until the 1.0.0 design review, a data.frame was rejected with a conversion hint, which hit tables from read.csv() on the first call.

  20. audit() reaches every tier. Sequence and total-n output carries the basic mapper’s class too, after its own tier classes, so the methods audit.scrutiny_map_seq() and audit.scrutiny_map_total_n() (R/audit.R) are what keep audit() from summarizing dispersed rows as reported cases. Study-level GRIM statistics, grim_binomial() and grim_plot_rates(), reject those tiers through check_grim_map_basic() for the same reason. Any new function that reads mapper output as a set of reported value sets needs the same guard.

  21. grim(), grimmer(), and debit() write out their own signatures. They used to be Vectorize(grim_scalar) and the like, which copies every formal of the wrapped function — including show_rec and show_reason, which only the mapper tier has any use for, and which are the only way to make a *_scalar() function return something other than a logical value. mapply() then simplified that list return into a matrix. The signatures are now hand-written, minus those arguments, and share one body: map_value_sets() (R/map-value-sets.R).

    A wrapper’s signature must mirror its *_scalar() function’s, because map_value_sets() forwards only the arguments the caller actually supplied and lets .fn’s own defaults apply to the rest. That one rule is what keeps a missing digits_x reaching grim_scalar() as missing, so that error_digits_missing() fires (gotcha 12 again, one tier up).

    along names the arguments to vectorize over. The split is the mapper tier’s own: key columns, .args_by_row, and helper columns are vectorized; everything that function_map() passes as a constant for the whole call (rounding, threshold, symmetric, x_meaning, formula, sd_meaning) must be length 1. Recycling of the along arguments follows the tidyverse rules and errors on a mismatch, where mapply() recycled anything into anything and merely warned.

    Which arguments were supplied is worked out with missing(), evaluated in the wrapper’s frame. Do not swap in match.call(): it is cheaper, but a wrapper reached through lapply() is called as FUN(X[[i]], ...), and matching that call fails with “… used in a situation where it does not exist”.

  22. check_newly_numeric()’s round() test is one-sided, and must stay that way. The check asks whether x fits in digits decimal places. x == round(x, digits) answers that some 200 times faster than counting the decimal places in as.character(x), which is what decimal_places_scalar() does with three regular expressions — once per key value per row, formerly the most expensive part of a mapper call (#92). The test only ever passes a value; whatever it leaves undecided falls through to the count, which is unchanged. Two cases depend on that fallback: a double that prints as a short decimal without being that decimal’s double (0.1 + 0.2 prints as "0.3"), and a value whose integer part is longer than the 15 significant digits as.character() renders. Never widen the test into a tolerance-based one: the tolerance that would forgive floating-point noise overlaps the differences the count treats as real, so the two would disagree above about 15 significant digits.

    The whole-number test for digits is inlined against WHOLE_NUMBER_TOLERANCE rather than calling is_whole_number(). That constant exists because the old default argument, .Machine$double.eps^0.5, was a list lookup plus a square root on every call — more than the arithmetic it is a tolerance for. is_decidable_n_items() writes the same test out twice for the same reason (gotcha 18).

    decimal_places_scalar() branches on is.character(x) so that a numeric value skips the "Inf"/"NaN" match, which only a string can fail, and skips the exponent regexes unless a fixed-string search finds an e or E first. Both are guards against work, not changes to what is counted; decimal_places() must keep agreeing with it, and the generated corpus in test-decimal-places.R is what checks that.

    An infinite x or sd is undecidable, like a missing one. It needs no branch here — round() returns it unchanged, so it passes — and grim_scalar(), grimmer_scalar(), and grim_sums_scalar() each return NA for it rather than letting it reach sum_range(), whose infinitely wide range read as GRIM-consistent. DEBIT needs no such branch: its input checks already confine x and sd to [0, 1].

  23. GRIMMER and DEBIT have no 2^53 limit of their own. A double holds whole numbers exactly only below 2^53, and a value set on a rounding bound gets either verdict if a comparison goes past it, so no such arithmetic may degrade to floating point. R/exact-arithmetic.R has two levels: compare_products(), product_difference(), and floor_product_ratio() (Dekker’s two-product) for products of two factors below 2^53, cheap enough for the common path, and big() with the big_*() functions for whole numbers of any size (base-2^24 limbs), used only when a factor or result passes 2^53. whole_*() functions take either: a value is a classed big() number exactly when it is at least 2^53. Bounds are put in lowest terms (lowest_terms()) first.

    GRIMMER works on each candidate sum s = n * q + r shifted to r: subtracting q from every value keeps the deviations, so the sums of squares depend on the SD alone, not on the mean (sum_squares_range_shifted()). grimmer_explain() and grimmer_values() show the unshifted sums of squares (grimmer_candidate_absolute()), which they can only do below 2^53; beyond, the explanation says so and grimmer_values() errors. The one refusal left is n from 2 to 4 with shifted sums of squares from 2^40 on (check_grimmer_attainable_exact()): an SD of about 3e5 to 1e6, which no study reports for so few values, and beyond which loeschian_between() takes seconds and gigabytes for n = 3. n = 1 is decided exactly at any size. Apart from that, a million candidate sums (check_enumeration_size()) are the limit, with the mean known or not; when the sums cover every remainder modulo n, only those within reach of the SD’s term are tried.

    Rule out unrealistic sizes rather than compute them. Where exactness at sizes no study reaches keeps causing defects or slow paths, refuse the input with an error instead of adding more machinery. GRIM’s own limit on x * n * 10^(digits_x + 1) (check_sum_range_exact(), also used by percentage_of()) comes from roundwork::sum_range() and remains.
